fullText:
Interesting insights about agent memory.

Might be worth a read if you are building memory systems for your agents.

Can an agent's memory make it fail tasks it would solve without memory?

KAIST researchers find that it can, and they call it memory-induced degradation.

The cause is how lessons are stored. They infer lessons from runs labeled only as success or failure, then save them without the run itself. When a lesson is wrong, the agent has no way to verify it.

The authors introduce WikiTrace, which stores each lesson as a short insight linked to a summary of why the run succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory. When an insight is vague, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed run, the agent follows the links with terminal tools before acting.

Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, PlanCraft, AppWorld, and tau3-bench retail, it scores 10.7 points above the agent without memory on average and 3.2 points above the same insights alone. The failure rate for previously solvable tasks drops from 6.5% to 4.5%.

https://t.co/3wU1elq35o

One of the most fun and productive periods of my career involved what I'd call "cooperative competition".

I was a postdoc in Toronto, working with Allan Jepson. He and I both had different methods for computing optical flow from video.

It was a like a dance. I would improve my method and run into his office with the new results. He'd then improve his method and run into my office with his results.

We were learning from each other and the competition drove each of us to be better. It was exciting and joyful.

If you find yourself in such a situation, enjoy it. I think it's rare. Put aside ego and have fun.

How to Win in Consumer Electronics: Lessons from Huawei and Xiaomi.

I like to go to Huawei’s product innovation events.

They are just really good (and fast) at hardware innovation.

But consumer electronics is a tough business.

So, how do you win?

My answer is 3 points.

Point 1: Win first with quality, utility and emotional resonance.

Huawei has new kids watch flips up for video calls. 

They have luxury smart watches for women.

They really focus on quality PLUS emotional resonance.

You need both. In the right use case.

Point 2: Long term, you need one of 2 plays

Ecosystem building. Think Xiaomi and their integrated phones, homes and cars.

or

Tech leadership. Think Huawei in hardware.

Point 3: Tech leadership in hardware is a marathon.

Huawei's MatePad Pro Max weighs 500 grams and is just 4.7 millimeters thick. 

That's crazy.

Their smartwatches can keep a charge for a week.

They are running a marathon in hardware breakthroughs. It's impressive.

fullText:
a16z's first employee Scott Kupor on how Michael Ovitz's CAA playbook became the model for a16z:

"When you would go show up for a pitch at CAA in 1990 where I think they had like 90% market share, they would sit around a table, and Michael would introduce you as Robert Redford and say, 'Look, meet my colleague who does nothing other than radio deals. Here's my expert in radio deals. Here's my expert in international. Here's my expert in books.'"

"And we basically took the same model to the VC world. The VC world was a lot like that. You had a one-to-one relationship with John Doerr, who was fantastic at what he did."

"As the domains grew, the expertise needed just continued to grow."

"Let's hire GPs who are functional domain experts in the particular areas of investing they want, and then let's surround them with this phalanx of somebody who all they do all day long is manage CFO relationships, or CEO relationships, or VPs of engineering, somebody who all they do is government relations, or business development."
